# Citation

Sinha, D., Maurya, A. K., Abdi, G., Majeed, M., Agarwal, R., Mukherjee, R., Ganguly, S., Aziz, R., Bhatia, M., Majgaonkar, A., Seal, S., Das, M., Banerjee, S., Chowdhury, S., Adeyemi, S. B., and Chen, J.-T. (2023). Integrated Genomic Selection for Accelerating Breeding Programs of Climate-Smart Cereals. *Genes* 14, 1484. https://doi.org/10.3390/genes14071484 (PDF p. 1).

# One-Sentence Summary

This review proposes integrating genomic selection with speed breeding, genotyping, phenotyping, sequencing and statistical tools to accelerate development of climate-smart cereal varieties (PDF pp. 1–26, Figures 1–4, Tables 1–2).

# Research Question

How can genomic selection and complementary breeding technologies be integrated to improve cereal yield and climate-stress adaptation? This paraphrases the abstract and review structure (PDF pp. 1–6).

# Biological System

Cereal crops, with examples including maize, barley, rice and wheat, and traits such as grain yield, drought response and stress tolerance (PDF pp. 10–16, Table 2). No new cereal experiment or breeding population was generated by the review.

# Study Design

Narrative review and framework article covering climate-smart crops, genomic selection methodology, breeding acceleration, genotyping, phenotyping and statistical tools (PDF pp. 2–26, Sections 1–11). A systematic search protocol, pooled analysis or newly implemented integrated pipeline: Not reported.

# Data

The review describes training and breeding populations, genotypes, phenotypes, high-throughput phenotyping data and next-generation sequencing inputs (PDF pp. 10–22, Sections 7–8). Table 2 summarizes published cereal model/trait improvements, including **GBLUP for maize grain yield** and **RRBLUP for barley grain yield** (PDF p. 15, Table 2). These are source-study examples, not new measurements.

# Methods

- Explain genomic selection and contrast it with marker-assisted selection (PDF pp. 7–11, Table 1, Figure 4).
- Discuss training-population design, statistical models and advanced breeding populations (PDF pp. 11–16, Sections 7.1–7.3).
- Review speed breeding, high-throughput genotyping, genotype imputation, high-throughput phenotyping and NGS (PDF pp. 16–22, Sections 8.1–8.7).
- Survey tools including Wheat Genomic Selection, GMStool, SolGS, BGLR, GenSel, STGS, MTGS and Ime4GS (PDF pp. 23–25, Section 9).

# Software and Versions

Named tools include **BGLR R-package**, **GenSel**, **SolGS**, **GMStool**, **STGS**, **MTGS** and **Ime4GS** (PDF pp. 23–25, Section 9). The article does not establish a common executed software environment or versions for the review's own analyses: Not reported.

# Important Parameters

The review emphasizes training-population size and composition, marker density, trait architecture, heritability, genotyping quality, imputation and model choice (PDF pp. 10–16, Sections 7.1–7.3). No universal marker filter, cross-validation split, model hyperparameter or stress-treatment threshold is prescribed. Numerical accuracies or crop-model pairings in Table 2 belong to cited studies (PDF p. 15, Table 2).

# Inputs and Outputs

Inputs include genotypes, phenotypes, training populations, environmental and high-throughput phenotyping data, and sequencing information. Outputs include genomic estimated breeding values, prediction accuracy, selection decisions and climate-adapted cereal candidates (PDF pp. 10–22, Sections 7–8). No unified output file is reported.

# Main Results

The authors argue that integrated genomic selection can accelerate breeding by combining prediction with speed breeding, high-throughput genotyping and phenotyping, NGS and advanced statistical tools (PDF pp. 16–26, Sections 8–11). The proposed framework is a review-level synthesis; Table 2 contains previously published crop-specific examples rather than a new common benchmark (PDF p. 15, Table 2).

# Assumptions

Integration assumes that training populations represent breeding targets and that genomic, phenotypic and environmental data can be combined without losing relevant biological signal (PDF pp. 10–16). Climate-smart selection also assumes that stress-response phenotypes are measured reliably across relevant environments (PDF pp. 5–7, 25–26).

# Limitations

The review identifies data quality, training-population design, model choice, environmental instability, implementation cost and the complexity of integrating multiple technologies as challenges (PDF pp. 10–11, 25–26). It provides no unified benchmark or original validation of the proposed integrated framework.

# Reproducible Implementation Details

No single genotype/phenotype data set, reference genome, filtering protocol, cross-validation design, software lockfile or model hyperparameters are supplied for a new integrated analysis: Not reported. Section 9 identifies tools, while the cited original studies must provide implementation details (PDF pp. 23–25).

# Relevance to simitall

**Inference, not an author recommendation:** This review could support simitall documentation of integrated plant genomic-selection workflows, especially for climate-stress and cereal breeding. It does not mention or evaluate simitall (PDF pp. 1–26).

# Terminology

- **Climate-smart cereal:** Cereal improvement target combining productivity with adaptation to climate-related stress (PDF pp. 5–7).
- **GS:** Genomic selection using genome-wide marker information for prediction and selection (PDF pp. 7–11).
- **HTP:** High-throughput phenotyping for rapid measurement of plant traits (PDF pp. 19–20).
- **GAB:** Genomics-assisted breeding discussed as an advanced breeding framework (PDF p. 16).

# References

Primary source: Sinha et al. (2023), cited above. The original studies summarized in Tables 1–2 and Section 9 appear in the References beginning on PDF p. 27. No outside sources were used.
